description:
What if your Moon landing slips one week?

At the south pole, the Sun barely rises. One ridge can leave you in the dark. GEOATHECMOON checks any site and date in seconds, with NASA Horizons and LOLA data. One week late, the battery runs out. Our AI proposes fixes; the simulator checks each one validated against NASA's illumination maps: six of six sites within five points.
summary:
GeoAthecmoon is a mission planner and simulator for the Moon's south pole. It answers the challenge's central question: if the mission is delayed, will it still work?

Users choose one of six known landing sites on an interactive 3D map, along with a date and mission length. For each hour of the mission, the tool checks whether the lander has sunlight for its solar panels, whether it can reach Earth, and how steep the ground is. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons, and the terrain comes from NASA LOLA. From these the tool gives a viability percentage and suggests a better site or date when one exists.

Users can then set up their lander (battery, panel, power use and data) and simulate the mission hour by hour. The result shows whether it survives, how much data it sends and how many days of delay it can tolerate. An AI rescue copilot tests recovery options when something goes wrong.

NASA's existing tools are powerful but hard to use. GeoAthecmoon makes this planning clear for engineers, students and the public, in English and Spanish.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

GEOATHECMOON helps plan a landing at the lunar south pole. The user picks one of 6 real sites (Shackleton rim, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache rim, Mons Mouton, Malapert Massif and Nobile rim), a date and the days on the surface. The app answers three questions hour by hour across all of 2027: does the site have sunlight for the solar panels, can it talk to Earth, and is the slope safe?

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun and Earth positions come from JPL Horizons for each site.

- The terrain comes from the LOLA digital elevation model (LDEM_80S_80M). For each site we trace a 150 km horizon that includes lunar curvature. There is light when the Sun is above that horizon, and contact when Earth is.

- The result is a 0–100 score that explains what limits it, plus the 3D terrain lit for that date.

- The simulator models the lander: solar power (1361 W/m² × area × efficiency × visible fraction of the solar disk), a battery with 0.90 charge and discharge efficiency that fails at 20%, and data sent only while Earth is visible.

- "What if the mission is delayed?" moves the landing date and simulates again. The result says how many days of delay the mission tolerates.

- A survival map shows 6 sites × 365 days with the same lander.

- If the mission fails, an AI rescue copilot proposes combinations (wait in orbit, change site, run fewer instruments) and the simulator checks every one. The AI never invents numbers.

VALIDATION

- Our % of sunlight is within 5 points of NASA's official LOLA illumination maps at all 6 sites (median 2.6 points).

- Connecting Ridge gets 89.5% sunlight over 2027, against 89% published by Mazarico et al. (2011).

- The calculation detects the penumbral lunar eclipse of August 17, 2027 as a partial solar eclipse seen from Malapert.

- An independent Python backend agrees within 0.5 points at 5 of 6 sites.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

NASA's tools (Moon Trek, QuickMap, Horizons) are powerful but hard to use. GEOATHECMOON turns the same data into a clear answer in seconds, so engineers can compare a plan against alternatives when the schedule changes, students can learn why the south pole is difficult, and the public can follow the logic of a landing decision. It works in English and Spanish.

TOOLS

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js with React Three Fiber for 3D.

- Backend and data pipeline: Python (NumPy, FastAPI, Matplotlib).

- AI copilot: OpenAI API through a server function, so the key never reaches the browser.

- Hosting: Vercel (app) and Render (data API).

- 3D models from NASA 3D Resources.

- Automated tests with Node's test runner.

CREATIVITY

The tool asks "what if we are late?" instead of only "is this site good?". It shows events in the 3D scene before showing statistics, and it explains which ridge blocks the Sun and how far away it is.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Ease of use for non-experts.

- Using only real NASA data, without inventing numbers.

- Being honest about limits. We do not model temperature, dust, battery degradation or relay satellites. Lander presets are illustrative. The Earth–Moon trip is an educational two-body model.

- The app keeps working without the backend or the AI.
